name: Ingestion
description: Bringing data into the lakehouse from source systems, streams, and files.

pillars.name: Governance
pillars.description: Govern data from the moment it enters the lakehouse so ingested assets are cataloged, classified, and traceable.

questions.title: Register ingested data in Unity Catalog at the point of entry
questions.details: Every source landing in the lakehouse should be registered as a Unity Catalog object as soon as it is ingested, so ownership, permissions, and metadata are attached from day one rather than retrofitted later.

databricksGuidance.context: Unity Catalog is the single place to govern ingested tables, volumes, and external locations. Registering sources on arrival keeps the catalog authoritative.

questions: Are landing/bronze tables registered in Unity Catalog?
Are external locations and volumes used for raw files governed by UC?
Is an owner assigned to every ingested dataset?

questions.title: Capture lineage from source systems into the lakehouse
questions.details: Automatically captured lineage from the ingestion layer downstream lets you trace any table back to the source system and file that produced it, which is essential for impact analysis and audits.

databricksGuidance.context: Unity Catalog captures lineage for pipelines that write through supported entry points; using them at ingestion means lineage starts at the source.

questions: Is lineage captured from ingestion pipelines to bronze tables?
Can you trace a table back to its originating source system?

questions.title: Classify and tag sensitive data as it is ingested
questions.details: Sensitive fields (PII, PCI, PHI) should be identified and tagged during ingestion so downstream masking and access policies can be applied consistently from the bronze layer onward.

databricksGuidance.context: Tagging at ingestion prevents sensitive data from spreading through the lakehouse untracked.

questions: Are sensitive columns tagged at ingestion?
Is there a process to classify new sources before they go live?

questions.title: Centralize access control for landing zones and ingestion pipelines
questions.details: Access to raw landing zones and the pipelines that write them should be governed centrally with least privilege, so only authorized principals can read source data or alter ingestion logic.

databricksGuidance.context: Centralized grants on external locations and bronze schemas keep raw data from becoming an ungoverned back door.

questions: Are permissions on landing zones managed in Unity Catalog?
Is access to raw data restricted to ingestion service principals and stewards?

questions.title: Define data quality standards for incoming data
questions.details: Document the quality expectations (completeness, format, freshness) that incoming data must meet before it is promoted past the bronze layer, so bad source data is caught at the boundary.

databricksGuidance.context: Agreeing quality standards for each source makes ingestion validation objective and enforceable.

questions: Are quality expectations documented per source?
Is there an agreed action for data that fails them (quarantine, reject, alert)?

pillars.name: Interoperability & Usability
pillars.description: Use standard connectors, open formats, and reusable patterns so new sources are easy to onboard.

questions.title: Use optimized connectors to ingest data sources
questions.details: Prefer managed, optimized connectors (Lakeflow Connect, partner connectors) over bespoke extraction code so ingestion from common sources is reliable and maintained.

databricksGuidance.context: Managed connectors reduce the custom code you own and keep pace with source-system changes.

questions: Are managed connectors used for common sources?
Is bespoke extraction code limited to sources without a connector?

questions.title: Use standard, reusable ingestion patterns
questions.details: Establish a small set of blessed ingestion patterns (batch file, CDC, streaming) that teams reuse, rather than every team inventing its own approach.

databricksGuidance.context: Reusable patterns make ingestion predictable to operate and onboard.

questions: Are there documented, reusable ingestion patterns?
Do new sources adopt an existing pattern by default?

questions.principle: Utilize open interfaces and data formats
questions.title: Land ingested data in open formats
questions.details: Write ingested data to open formats (Delta / Parquet) so it stays portable and queryable by any engine, avoiding lock-in at the raw layer.

databricksGuidance.context: Open formats at the landing layer keep the lakehouse interoperable end to end.

questions: Is ingested data written to Delta or another open format?

questions.title: Use certified partner tools for ingestion
questions.details: Where a partner ingestion tool is already in use, prefer certified integrations validated against Databricks so support and compatibility are assured.

databricksGuidance.context: Certified partner tools are tested against the platform and reduce integration risk.

questions: Are partner ingestion tools certified for Databricks?
Is Partner Connect used to configure them where possible?

questions.title: Offer a self-service path to onboard new sources
questions.details: Provide a self-service, templated way for teams to onboard a new source (request, configure, deploy) so ingestion is not a bottleneck owned by one team.

databricksGuidance.context: Self-service onboarding scales ingestion across the organization.

questions: Can teams onboard a new source without a central bottleneck?
Are templates provided for common source types?

pillars.name: Operational Excellence
pillars.description: Automate, version, and monitor ingestion pipelines so they run hands-off and are easy to change safely.

questions.title: Use automated, event-driven file ingestion
questions.details: Use Auto Loader to incrementally and automatically ingest new files as they arrive, rather than scheduling full directory rescans, so ingestion is efficient and hands-off.

databricksGuidance.context: Auto Loader tracks which files have been processed and scales to high file volumes without manual bookkeeping.

questions: Is Auto Loader used for file-based ingestion?
Is file notification mode used for high-volume sources?

questions.title: Use a declarative ETL framework for ingestion pipelines
questions.details: Build ingestion pipelines with a declarative framework (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines / DLT) so dependencies, retries, and data quality are handled by the framework instead of hand-written orchestration.

databricksGuidance.context: Declarative pipelines reduce boilerplate and build in reliability features for ingestion.

questions: Are data quality expectations defined in the pipeline?

questions.title: Manage ingestion pipeline code in source control with CI/CD
questions.details: Ingestion pipeline definitions should live in version control and deploy through CI/CD across environments, so changes are reviewed, tested, and reproducible.

databricksGuidance.context: Treating ingestion as code prevents drift between dev and production pipelines.

questions: Is ingestion pipeline code in an SCM repository?
Are pipelines deployed via CI/CD rather than edited in production?

questions.principle: Set up Monitoring, Alerting and Logging
questions.title: Monitor ingestion pipelines and alert on failures
questions.details: Ingestion pipelines should emit metrics (records ingested, failures, latency) and raise alerts when a source stops arriving or a run fails, so gaps are caught before they reach consumers.

databricksGuidance.context: A silent ingestion failure is often only noticed downstream; proactive alerting shortens time to detect.

questions: Are ingestion runs monitored for failures and latency?
Are alerts raised when an expected source stops arriving?

questions.title: Manage source connection limits and API quotas
questions.details: Understand and respect the rate limits and connection quotas of source systems and cloud APIs so ingestion does not throttle or overwhelm the source.

databricksGuidance.context: Ingestion that ignores source quotas causes throttling, backpressure, and failed runs.

questions: Are source API rate limits known and respected?
Is ingestion concurrency tuned to source capacity?

pillars.name: Security, Compliance & Privacy
pillars.description: Protect source credentials, landing storage, and data in transit as it enters the lakehouse.

questions.principle: Manage identity and access using least privilege
questions.title: Store source-system credentials with secret management
questions.details: Credentials for source databases, APIs, and message buses must be held in a secret store and referenced by ingestion jobs, never hard-coded in pipeline code or notebooks.

databricksGuidance.context: Secret management keeps source credentials out of code and logs.

questions: Are source credentials stored in a secret scope?
Is pipeline code free of hard-coded credentials?

questions.principle: Protect data in transit and at rest
questions.title: Secure access to landing cloud storage
questions.details: Landing buckets/containers should be reachable only through governed external locations with least-privilege cloud IAM, not broad or public access.

databricksGuidance.context: The raw landing zone is a common weak point; lock it down like production storage.

questions: Is landing storage accessed via governed external locations?
Are cloud IAM permissions on landing storage least-privilege?

questions.principle: Protect data in transit and at rest
questions.title: Encrypt data in transit from source systems
questions.details: Connections to source systems should use TLS so data is encrypted in transit as it is pulled into the lakehouse.

databricksGuidance.context: In-transit encryption protects source data on the wire during ingestion.

questions: Are source connections encrypted with TLS?
Are unencrypted protocols disabled for ingestion?

questions.principle: Manage identity and access using least privilege
questions.title: Run production ingestion jobs as service principals
questions.details: Scheduled ingestion should run under service principals rather than individual user identities, so pipelines are not tied to a person and permissions stay scoped.

databricksGuidance.context: Service principals decouple production ingestion from personal accounts.

questions: Do production ingestion jobs run as service principals?
Are those principals scoped to only the sources they need?

questions.principle: Secure your network and identify and protect endpoints
questions.title: Apply network controls to ingestion connectivity
questions.details: Where sources are reached over the network, use private connectivity and egress controls so ingestion traffic does not traverse the public internet unnecessarily.

databricksGuidance.context: Private connectivity for ingestion reduces exposure and supports exfiltration controls.

questions: Is private connectivity used to reach sources where possible?
Are egress controls applied to ingestion compute?

pillars.name: Reliability
pillars.description: Ingest resiliently: rescue bad records, retry safely, and recover streaming pipelines without data loss.

questions.title: Automatically rescue invalid or nonconforming incoming data
questions.details: Malformed or unexpected incoming records should be captured in a rescued-data column or quarantine rather than failing the whole run or being silently dropped.

databricksGuidance.context: Rescuing bad records keeps ingestion flowing while preserving the data for later inspection.

questions: Are nonconforming records rescued or quarantined?
Is rescued data reviewed rather than ignored?

questions.title: Configure ingestion jobs for automatic retries and timeouts
questions.details: Ingestion jobs should retry transient source failures automatically and time out hung tasks, so a brief source outage does not require manual intervention and a stuck run does not cost indefinitely.

databricksGuidance.context: Retries and timeouts balance reliability against runaway cost for ingestion.

questions: Are automatic retries configured for ingestion jobs?
Are timeouts set to terminate hung ingestion tasks?

questions.title: Recover streaming ingestion from checkpoint failures
questions.details: Streaming ingestion must use checkpointing so a failed query can resume exactly where it left off, and recovery from a lost or corrupt checkpoint should be a tested procedure.

databricksGuidance.context: Checkpoints make streaming ingestion restartable without reprocessing or data loss.

questions: Do streaming ingestion queries use checkpoints?
Has recovery from checkpoint loss been tested?

questions.title: Enforce schema on incoming data
questions.details: Ingestion should enforce or explicitly evolve schema so unexpected source changes are detected at the boundary rather than corrupting downstream tables.

databricksGuidance.context: Schema enforcement at ingestion turns silent source drift into a visible, handled event.

questions: Is schema enforced on incoming data?
Is schema evolution handled explicitly and reviewed?

questions.title: Enable autoscaling for ingestion workloads
questions.details: Ingestion compute should scale with incoming volume so bursts are absorbed without manual resizing and quiet periods do not waste resources.

databricksGuidance.context: Autoscaling matches ingestion capacity to variable source volume.

questions: Is autoscaling enabled for ingestion compute?
Are min/max bounds tuned to expected volume?

pillars.name: Performance Efficiency
pillars.description: Ingest incrementally and size files well so the landing layer is fast and cheap to read downstream.

questions.title: Understand your ingestion patterns and access needs
questions.details: Know whether each source is batch or streaming, its volume and velocity, and how fresh consumers need it, so the ingestion design fits the actual pattern rather than a default.

databricksGuidance.context: Matching ingestion design to the real pattern avoids both over-engineering and missed SLAs.

questions: Is each source characterized as batch or streaming?
Are freshness requirements known per source?

questions.title: Ingest incrementally rather than reprocessing full loads
questions.details: Prefer incremental ingestion of only new or changed data over repeated full reloads, which waste compute and slow the landing layer.

databricksGuidance.context: Incremental ingestion keeps cost and latency proportional to new data, not total data.

questions: Is ingestion incremental where the source supports it?
Are full reloads limited to genuine backfills?

questions.title: Avoid the small-file problem at the landing layer
questions.details: Many tiny files from high-frequency sources degrade downstream read performance; tune batch sizes or compact on write so landed data is well-sized.

databricksGuidance.context: File sizing at ingestion determines how efficient every downstream read is.

questions: Are landed files a reasonable size rather than many tiny files?
Is compaction applied where sources produce small files?

questions.title: Use serverless compute for ingestion where appropriate
questions.details: Serverless compute can start fast and scale for spiky ingestion without managing clusters, which suits event-driven and intermittent sources.

databricksGuidance.context: Serverless removes cluster management overhead for bursty ingestion.

questions: Is serverless considered for intermittent ingestion?
Are workloads matched to serverless vs classic appropriately?

questions.title: Monitor ingestion throughput and latency
questions.details: Track how fast data moves from source to landing and whether latency meets freshness SLAs, so degradation is caught and tuned.

databricksGuidance.context: Throughput and latency metrics show whether ingestion keeps up with the source.

questions: Is end-to-end ingestion latency tracked against SLAs?

pillars.name: Cost Optimization
pillars.description: Ingest with right-sized, ephemeral compute and attribute ingestion cost so spend stays proportional to data.

questions.title: Use job clusters for scheduled ingestion
questions.details: Scheduled ingestion should run on ephemeral job clusters that spin up for the run and terminate after, rather than on always-on all-purpose compute.

databricksGuidance.context: Job clusters avoid paying for idle all-purpose compute between ingestion runs.

questions: Does scheduled ingestion use job clusters?
Is all-purpose compute avoided for production ingestion?

questions.title: Balance always-on streaming against triggered ingestion
questions.details: For sources that do not need continuous processing, triggered (incremental batch) ingestion can deliver the required freshness at a fraction of always-on streaming cost.

databricksGuidance.context: Matching the trigger mode to freshness needs is one of the biggest ingestion cost levers.

questions: Is always-on streaming reserved for sources that truly need it?
Is triggered ingestion used where periodic freshness suffices?

questions.title: Auto-terminate ingestion compute when idle
questions.details: Ingestion compute should auto-terminate when not in use so idle clusters do not accrue cost between runs.

databricksGuidance.context: Auto-termination is a simple guard against forgotten, idle ingestion compute.

questions: Is auto-termination configured on ingestion compute?

questions.title: Tag and attribute ingestion costs
questions.details: Tag ingestion compute by source or team so its cost can be attributed and charged back, making expensive sources visible.

databricksGuidance.context: Cost attribution turns ingestion spend into something owners can see and optimize.

questions: Is ingestion compute tagged for cost attribution?
Can ingestion cost be broken down by source or team?

questions.title: Land data in performance-optimized open formats
questions.details: Writing landed data in an efficient columnar open format (Delta) reduces the cost of every downstream read compared with raw text formats.

databricksGuidance.context: The landing format sets a cost floor for all downstream processing.

questions: Is landed data stored in Delta rather than raw CSV/JSON long-term?
Are raw text formats converted early in the pipeline?

name: Storage
description: Persisting data durably and efficiently across the lakehouse.

pillars.name: Governance
pillars.description: Govern where and how data is stored, with clear ownership and retention.

questions.title: Organize storage with a Unity Catalog namespace strategy
questions.details: Define a catalog/schema strategy so stored data has a consistent, governed namespace rather than ad-hoc locations.

databricksGuidance.context: A deliberate catalog hierarchy keeps stored data discoverable and permissioned.

questions: Is there a documented catalog/schema strategy?
Are stored tables placed in the right catalog by domain/environment?

questions.title: Manage metadata and descriptions for stored tables
questions.details: Stored tables and columns should carry descriptions and metadata so consumers understand what is persisted.

databricksGuidance.context: Well-described storage is the difference between a data asset and a data swamp.

questions.title: Centralize access control on stored data
questions.details: Read/write access to stored tables and volumes should be governed centrally with least privilege.

databricksGuidance.context: Central grants keep persisted data from being over-shared.

questions: Are grants on stored data managed in Unity Catalog?
Is least privilege applied to storage?

questions.title: Define retention and lifecycle policies for stored data
questions.details: Document how long each dataset is kept and when it is archived or deleted, so storage does not grow unbounded and compliance is met.

databricksGuidance.context: Retention policy governs both cost and compliance of stored data.

questions: Are retention periods defined per dataset?
Is old data archived or purged on schedule?

questions.title: Classify sensitive stored data for masking
questions.details: Sensitive columns in stored tables should be tagged so masking and row/column-level policies apply consistently.

databricksGuidance.context: Classification at rest enables consistent protection of stored PII.

questions: Are sensitive columns tagged in storage?
Are masking policies applied from those tags?

pillars.name: Interoperability & Usability
pillars.description: Store in open formats behind open interfaces so data stays portable and shareable.

questions.principle: Utilize open interfaces and data formats
questions.title: Store data in Delta Lake
questions.details: Persist tables in Delta so storage is ACID, time-travel capable, and portable across engines.

databricksGuidance.context: Delta is the open, transactional storage foundation of the lakehouse.

questions: Is stored data in Delta format?

questions.principle: Utilize open interfaces and data formats
questions.title: Enable secure sharing of stored data
questions.details: Use Delta Sharing to expose stored datasets to other teams or organizations without copying data.

databricksGuidance.context: Open sharing avoids proprietary export/copy sprawl of stored data.

questions: Is Delta Sharing used to share stored data?

questions.title: Publish curated stored data as reusable data products
questions.details: Promote well-modeled stored tables as data products the business can trust and reuse, rather than raw dumps.

databricksGuidance.context: Data-product thinking makes stored data consumable.

questions: Are curated tables published as products?
Do they have clear owners and contracts?

questions.title: Use a central catalog for discovery of stored data
questions.details: Stored data should be discoverable through a central catalog with search and lineage.

databricksGuidance.context: Discovery turns storage into something teams can find and reuse.

questions: Is stored data discoverable via the catalog?
Is lineage visible for stored tables?

questions.title: Keep stored data semantically consistent across domains
questions.details: Shared dimensions and definitions should be consistent across stored datasets so they join and reconcile.

databricksGuidance.context: Semantic consistency prevents conflicting versions of the truth at rest.

questions: Are shared definitions consistent across stored tables?

pillars.name: Operational Excellence
pillars.description: Maintain stored data automatically: optimize, vacuum, and monitor growth.

questions.title: Automate table maintenance (OPTIMIZE, VACUUM)
questions.details: Storage maintenance like compaction and vacuum should run automatically rather than manually, ideally via Predictive Optimization.

databricksGuidance.context: Automated maintenance keeps stored tables healthy without manual chores.

questions: Is Predictive Optimization enabled where available?

questions.principle: Set up Monitoring, Alerting and Logging
questions.title: Monitor storage growth and table health
questions.details: Track table sizes, file counts, and growth so storage issues are caught before they degrade performance or cost.

databricksGuidance.context: Monitoring growth prevents surprise storage bills and small-file decay.

questions: Are file-count/health metrics tracked per table?

questions.title: Manage schema changes to stored tables through change control
questions.details: Changes to stored table schemas should go through version-controlled, reviewed processes to avoid breaking consumers.

databricksGuidance.context: Controlled schema evolution protects downstream consumers of stored data.

questions: Are breaking changes communicated to consumers?

questions.title: Use a layered (medallion) storage architecture
questions.details: Organize stored data into bronze/silver/gold layers so raw, refined, and curated data are cleanly separated.

databricksGuidance.context: A layered architecture makes stored data governable and reusable.

questions: Are layers clearly separated and owned?

questions.title: Plan storage capacity and quotas
questions.details: Understand storage growth trends and cloud account quotas so capacity is planned rather than hit as a limit.

databricksGuidance.context: Capacity planning avoids storage-related outages and rushed cleanups.

pillars.name: Security, Compliance & Privacy
pillars.description: Protect stored data with encryption, key management, and least-privilege storage access.

questions.principle: Protect data in transit and at rest
questions.title: Encrypt stored data and restrict access
questions.details: Data at rest should be encrypted and access to underlying cloud storage restricted to governed paths.

databricksGuidance.context: Encryption at rest is a baseline control for stored data.

questions: Is stored data encrypted at rest?

questions.principle: Protect data in transit and at rest
questions.title: Use customer-managed keys where required
questions.details: For regulated data, consider customer-managed encryption keys so key rotation and revocation are under your control.

databricksGuidance.context: CMK gives control over the encryption lifecycle of stored data.

questions: Are customer-managed keys used where required?

questions.principle: Protect data in transit and at rest
questions.title: Avoid storing production data in DBFS root
questions.details: Production data should live in governed external locations or managed storage, not the DBFS root.

databricksGuidance.context: The DBFS root is not a safe home for production data.

questions: Is production data kept out of DBFS root?

questions.principle: Protect data in transit and at rest
questions.title: Enable storage versioning for recovery
questions.details: Bucket/container versioning protects stored data against accidental deletion or corruption.

databricksGuidance.context: Versioning is a cheap safety net for stored data.

questions: Is object versioning enabled on storage?
Is there a recovery process using it?

questions.principle: Meet compliance and data privacy requirements
questions.title: Support data deletion and privacy requests on stored data
questions.details: Stored data must support deletion/erasure requests (e.g. GDPR) so privacy obligations can be met.

databricksGuidance.context: Privacy law requires that stored personal data can be found and deleted.

questions: Can personal data be located and deleted on request?

pillars.name: Reliability
pillars.description: Keep stored data durable and recoverable through ACID, backups, and time travel.

questions.title: Use a storage format that supports ACID transactions
questions.details: ACID storage prevents partial writes and corruption when jobs fail mid-write.

databricksGuidance.context: ACID guarantees keep stored tables consistent through failures.

questions: Does stored data use an ACID format?

questions.title: Recover stored data using time travel
questions.details: Time travel lets you restore a stored table to a previous version after a bad write or delete.

databricksGuidance.context: Time travel is the first line of recovery for stored tables.

questions: Is Delta time travel available for recovery?
Has restoring a prior version been tested?

questions.title: Configure a disaster-recovery pattern for storage
questions.details: Critical stored data should be replicated or backed up to support recovery from a regional failure.

databricksGuidance.context: DR for storage protects against loss of a region or account.

questions: Is critical stored data replicated for DR?

questions.title: Enforce constraints on stored tables
questions.details: Use table constraints and expectations so invalid data cannot be persisted.

databricksGuidance.context: Constraints keep stored data trustworthy.

questions: Are constraints/expectations defined on stored tables?

questions.title: Reduce redundancy in stored data
questions.details: Avoid uncontrolled copies of stored datasets, which drift and inflate cost; prefer a single governed source.

databricksGuidance.context: Redundant copies of stored data are a reliability and cost liability.

questions: Are uncontrolled copies of data avoided?
Is there a single source of truth per dataset?

pillars.name: Performance Efficiency
pillars.description: Lay out stored data for fast reads: clustering, file sizing, and data skipping.

questions.title: Cluster stored data for common query patterns
questions.details: Use liquid clustering or partitioning aligned to how stored data is queried, so reads skip irrelevant data.

databricksGuidance.context: Data layout is the biggest lever on stored-data read performance.

questions: Is stored data clustered/partitioned for query patterns?
Is liquid clustering used where suitable?

questions.title: Maintain healthy file sizes in storage
questions.details: Compact small files and avoid over-partitioning so stored tables read efficiently.

databricksGuidance.context: File sizing directly determines scan efficiency.

questions.title: Enable data skipping and statistics on stored tables
questions.details: Collect statistics so the engine can skip files that cannot match a query.

databricksGuidance.context: Data skipping turns storage layout into query speed.

questions: Is data skipping effective for common filters?

questions.title: Enable Predictive Optimization for stored tables
questions.details: Let the platform automatically apply the right layout optimizations to stored tables.

databricksGuidance.context: Predictive Optimization keeps layout tuned without manual effort.

questions.title: Monitor read performance on stored tables
questions.details: Track query performance against stored tables to catch layout degradation over time.

databricksGuidance.context: Monitoring reveals when stored data needs re-optimizing.

questions: Is read performance on key tables monitored?

pillars.name: Cost Optimization
pillars.description: Control storage cost with efficient formats, lifecycle tiering, and cleanup.

questions.title: Store data in performance-optimized formats
questions.details: Efficient columnar storage reduces both storage footprint and read cost.

databricksGuidance.context: The storage format sets a cost floor for every query.

questions: Are bloated raw formats avoided at rest?

questions.title: Vacuum and clean up obsolete stored files
questions.details: Remove obsolete data files and old versions so you do not pay to store data nothing reads.

databricksGuidance.context: Uncleaned history quietly inflates storage cost.

questions: Is VACUUM run on a schedule?
Are retention windows tuned to need?

questions.title: Tier cold data to cheaper storage
questions.details: Infrequently accessed stored data can move to lower-cost storage tiers.

databricksGuidance.context: Lifecycle tiering matches storage cost to access frequency.

questions: Is cold data moved to cheaper tiers?

questions.title: Attribute storage cost by owner
questions.details: Attribute storage consumption to teams/datasets so owners see and manage their footprint.

databricksGuidance.context: Attribution makes storage cost actionable.

questions: Can storage cost be attributed to owners?

questions.title: Monitor Delta Sharing egress costs
questions.details: Sharing stored data across regions/clouds can incur egress; monitor and manage it.

databricksGuidance.context: Egress from shared storage is an easily missed cost.

name: Processing
description: Transforming and enriching data through batch and streaming pipelines.

pillars.name: Governance
pillars.description: Govern transformations so processed data is traceable, documented, and quality-checked.

questions.title: Capture lineage through transformation pipelines
questions.details: Transformations should produce column-level lineage so processed outputs can be traced back to their inputs.

databricksGuidance.context: Transformation lineage is essential for impact analysis and trust in processed data.

questions: Is column-level lineage available for processed tables?

questions.title: Enforce data quality expectations during processing
questions.details: Processing pipelines should assert data quality expectations and act on violations, not just transform blindly.

databricksGuidance.context: Quality gates in processing stop bad data from propagating.

questions: Are quality expectations defined in pipelines?
Are violations quarantined or failed explicitly?

questions.title: Document transformation logic and business rules
questions.details: The business meaning of each transformation should be documented so processed data is interpretable.

databricksGuidance.context: Undocumented transformations become black boxes over time.

questions: Are business rules discoverable by consumers?

questions.title: Apply masking/row filters within processing
questions.details: Sensitive data should be masked or filtered as part of processing so downstream outputs respect policy.

databricksGuidance.context: Enforcing policy during processing keeps sensitive data from leaking into curated outputs.

questions: Are masking/row filters applied in processing?
Do processed outputs respect classification tags?

questions.title: Standardize formats and definitions in transformations
questions.details: Processing should normalize data to standard formats and shared definitions so outputs are consistent.

databricksGuidance.context: Standardization during processing produces conformed, reconcilable data.

pillars.name: Interoperability & Usability
pillars.description: Build transformations on open engines and reusable, low-complexity patterns.

questions.title: Reduce complexity of transformation pipelines
questions.details: Prefer declarative transformation frameworks over sprawling imperative code so pipelines stay simple to build and change.

databricksGuidance.context: Lower pipeline complexity means faster, safer changes.

questions: Are declarative frameworks used for transformations?

questions.principle: Utilize open interfaces and data formats
questions.title: Use open, standard processing engines
questions.details: Build transformations on open engines (Spark, SQL) so logic is portable and not locked to a proprietary tool.

databricksGuidance.context: Open engines keep processing logic portable.

questions: Is processing built on open engines?

questions.title: Use serverless compute for transformations
questions.details: Serverless processing removes cluster management and scales with the workload.

databricksGuidance.context: Serverless simplifies running transformations.

questions: Is serverless used for suitable transformations?

questions.title: Reuse standard transformation patterns
questions.details: Common transformation patterns (SCD, dedup, CDC apply) should be standardized and reused.

databricksGuidance.context: Reusable patterns keep processing consistent and maintainable.

questions.title: Use AI assistance to build transformations
questions.details: AI assistance can speed up writing and reviewing transformation code.

databricksGuidance.context: AI assistance increases processing productivity.

questions: Is AI assistance available to pipeline developers?

pillars.name: Operational Excellence
pillars.description: Automate, version, and observe transformation pipelines end to end.

questions.title: Use ETL frameworks for transformation pipelines
questions.details: Transformations should run on a managed ETL framework that handles dependencies, retries, and quality.

databricksGuidance.context: A framework removes hand-rolled orchestration from processing.

questions: Are pipelines built on an ETL framework?

questions.title: Version and CI/CD transformation code
questions.details: Transformation code should live in source control and deploy via CI/CD across environments.

databricksGuidance.context: Processing-as-code prevents environment drift.

questions.principle: Set up Monitoring, Alerting and Logging
questions.title: Monitor pipeline runs and data freshness
questions.details: Track processing run status, duration, and output freshness, and alert on failures or staleness.

databricksGuidance.context: Monitoring processing catches broken or late data early.

questions.title: Isolate dev, staging, and production for processing
questions.details: Transformations should run against isolated environments so development cannot affect production data.

databricksGuidance.context: Environment isolation protects production processing.

questions: Is production data protected from dev pipelines?

questions.title: Use declarative management for complex pipelines
questions.details: Complex multi-step transformations benefit from declarative dependency management over manual sequencing.

databricksGuidance.context: Declarative management scales complex processing.

pillars.name: Security, Compliance & Privacy
pillars.description: Secure processing compute, credentials, and intermediate data.

questions.principle: Manage identity and access using least privilege
questions.title: Run transformation jobs as service principals
questions.details: Production processing should run under scoped service principals, not personal accounts.

databricksGuidance.context: Service principals decouple production processing from individuals.

questions: Do processing jobs run as service principals?

questions.principle: Manage identity and access using least privilege
questions.title: Use compute that supports user isolation
questions.details: Shared processing compute should isolate users so one workload cannot access another’s data.

questions.principle: Manage identity and access using least privilege
questions.title: Scope AI endpoint access and credentials
questions.details: Endpoints and the credentials/tools they use should be least-privilege and secret-managed.

databricksGuidance.context: Over-privileged AI tools expand what a compromised app can do.

questions.principle: Meet compliance and data privacy requirements
questions.title: Meet compliance and content-safety requirements
questions.details: Generative apps must meet content-safety and regulatory requirements for their domain.

databricksGuidance.context: Compliance and safety obligations apply fully to generative output.

questions.title: Audit AI interactions
questions.details: Prompts, responses, and tool calls should be auditable for security and compliance review.

databricksGuidance.context: An audit trail of AI interactions supports investigation and compliance.

questions: Are AI interactions logged and auditable?

pillars.name: Reliability
pillars.description: Serve generative apps reliably with scalable, fault-tolerant endpoints and fallbacks.

questions.title: Use scalable, production-grade model serving
questions.details: Generative endpoints should run on production-grade serving that handles scale and failures.

databricksGuidance.context: Robust serving keeps generative apps available under load.

questions.title: Handle provider failures with retries and fallbacks
questions.details: Apps should retry and fall back to an alternate model/provider when one fails or rate-limits.

databricksGuidance.context: Fallbacks keep generative apps up when a provider degrades.

questions.title: Autoscale AI endpoints to demand
questions.details: Serving should scale with request volume, including scale-to-zero for intermittent apps.

databricksGuidance.context: Autoscaling matches generative capacity to demand.

questions.title: Guard against hallucination with grounding checks
questions.details: Groundedness checks and retrieval validation should reduce hallucinated or unsupported answers.

databricksGuidance.context: Grounding checks are the reliability control for generative correctness.

questions.title: Detect and respond to AI quality degradation
questions.details: Drops in answer quality or spikes in errors should trigger alerts and response.

databricksGuidance.context: Detecting degradation keeps a drifting generative app from misleading users.

pillars.name: Performance Efficiency
pillars.description: Make generative apps performant: retrieval, caching, and right-sized models.

questions.title: Use serverless serving for elastic AI performance
questions.details: Serverless serving scales generative endpoints without managing infrastructure.

databricksGuidance.context: Serverless serving handles variable generative load efficiently.

questions.title: Optimize retrieval for RAG latency
questions.details: Vector indexes and retrieval should be tuned so RAG apps respond quickly.

databricksGuidance.context: Retrieval is often the latency bottleneck in RAG apps.

questions: Is vector retrieval tuned for latency?

questions.title: Cache responses and embeddings where possible
questions.details: Caching repeated prompts/embeddings reduces latency and model calls.

databricksGuidance.context: Caching cuts both latency and cost for generative apps.

questions.title: Right-size the model to the task
questions.details: Use the smallest model that meets quality needs so latency and cost stay low.

databricksGuidance.context: Model right-sizing balances quality against speed and cost.

questions: Is the model right-sized to the task?

questions.title: Monitor endpoint latency and throughput
questions.details: Track token latency and throughput so generative performance stays within SLA.

databricksGuidance.context: Latency/throughput monitoring keeps generative UX acceptable.

pillars.name: Cost Optimization
pillars.description: Control generative-app cost via model choice, caching, and token management.

questions.title: Match model choice to cost/quality needs
questions.details: Choose models by cost-per-quality for each use case rather than defaulting to the largest.

databricksGuidance.context: Model selection is the biggest generative cost lever.

questions: Are models chosen by cost/quality fit?
Are premium models reserved for where they pay off?

questions.title: Cache to reduce token consumption
questions.details: Caching repeated prompts/responses avoids paying for the same generation twice.

databricksGuidance.context: Caching directly reduces token spend.

questions: Is caching used to cut token use?

questions.title: Only use GPUs where they are justified
questions.details: Reserve GPU-backed serving for workloads that genuinely need it.

databricksGuidance.context: Unjustified GPU serving is a common generative overspend.

questions: Is GPU serving reserved for workloads that need it?

questions.title: Track and attribute token/endpoint cost
questions.details: Token usage and endpoint cost should be tracked and attributable to apps/teams, with rate limits to bound spend.

databricksGuidance.context: Token cost is easy to lose track of without attribution and limits.

questions: Is token/endpoint cost tracked per app?
Are rate limits set to bound spend?

questions.title: Scale endpoints to zero when idle
questions.details: Intermittent generative endpoints should scale to zero so idle serving is not billed.

databricksGuidance.context: Scale-to-zero avoids paying for idle generative endpoints.

questions: Do intermittent endpoints scale to zero?

name: ML
description: Developing, training, and operating machine learning models.

pillars.name: Governance
pillars.description: Govern the ML lifecycle: features, models, and training data with lineage.

questions.title: Register models and features in Unity Catalog
questions.details: Models and features should be governed in the catalog so ownership, versions, and access are managed centrally.

databricksGuidance.context: Cataloging ML assets gives one governed view of models and features.

questions: Are models registered in Unity Catalog?
Are features governed in a feature store?

questions.title: Track lineage from training data to model
questions.details: Lineage should connect training datasets and features to the model versions they produced.

databricksGuidance.context: Model lineage is essential for reproducibility, audits, and debugging.

questions: Is lineage captured from data/features to models?
Can a model be traced to its training data?

questions.title: Control access to models, features, and training data
questions.details: Access to models, feature tables, and sensitive training data should follow least privilege.

databricksGuidance.context: Uncontrolled model/feature access is both a security and IP risk.

questions.title: Ensure quality of training data
questions.details: Training data should meet documented quality standards, since data issues propagate into model behavior.

databricksGuidance.context: Model quality is bounded by training-data quality.

questions: Are data issues caught before training?

questions.title: Maintain model documentation and cards
questions.details: Each model should have documentation (intended use, metrics, limitations) so it is used responsibly.

databricksGuidance.context: Model cards make model behavior and limits transparent.

questions: Are intended use and limitations recorded?

pillars.name: Interoperability & Usability
pillars.description: Build ML on open frameworks with reusable features and self-service tooling.

questions.principle: Utilize open interfaces and data formats
questions.title: Use open ML frameworks and formats
questions.details: Models and experiments should use open frameworks/formats (MLflow) so they are portable.

databricksGuidance.context: Open formats keep models portable across tools and environments.

questions.title: Share reusable features via a feature store
questions.details: Features should be published for reuse so teams do not re-engineer the same signals.

databricksGuidance.context: A feature store prevents duplicated, inconsistent feature engineering.

questions: Are features shared via a feature store?

questions.title: Provide self-service ML development environments
questions.details: Data scientists should have self-service, governed environments to develop models.

databricksGuidance.context: Self-service environments accelerate ML without losing governance.

questions.title: Use AutoML to accelerate baselines
questions.details: AutoML can produce strong baselines quickly and generate reproducible starter code.

databricksGuidance.context: AutoML shortens time to a first credible model.

questions: Is AutoML used for baselines where useful?

questions.title: Use consistent, pre-defined compute for ML
questions.details: Standard ML compute templates simplify moving from development to training.

databricksGuidance.context: Consistent compute reduces friction across the ML lifecycle.

questions: Are standard ML compute templates used?

pillars.name: Operational Excellence
pillars.description: Operate ML with MLOps: tracked experiments, registered models, deploy-code.

questions.title: Standardize MLOps processes across teams
questions.details: A consistent MLOps process (dev → staging → prod) should apply across ML teams.

databricksGuidance.context: Standard MLOps makes model delivery repeatable and reviewable.

questions: Is a standard MLOps process defined?

questions.title: Automate experiment tracking
questions.details: Experiments (params, metrics, artifacts) should be tracked automatically for comparison and reproducibility.

databricksGuidance.context: Automatic tracking makes ML experiments comparable and reproducible.

questions.title: Follow the deploy-code approach for ML
questions.details: Promote code (that trains the model) across environments rather than promoting model artifacts alone.

databricksGuidance.context: Deploy-code makes ML promotions reproducible and testable.

questions.title: Use a model registry to manage the model lifecycle
questions.details: A registry should decouple model versions from code and manage stage transitions.

databricksGuidance.context: The registry is the control point for the model lifecycle.

questions.principle: Set up Monitoring, Alerting and Logging
questions.title: Monitor models for drift and performance
questions.details: Production models should be monitored for data/prediction drift and quality, with alerting and retraining triggers.

databricksGuidance.context: Drift monitoring is how you learn a model has gone stale.

pillars.name: Security, Compliance & Privacy
pillars.description: Secure ML: protect training data, credentials, and served models.

questions.principle: Manage identity and access using least privilege
questions.title: Run training and serving as service principals
questions.details: Production ML jobs and endpoints should run under scoped service principals.

databricksGuidance.context: Service principals decouple production ML from individuals.

questions: Do ML jobs/endpoints run as service principals?

questions.principle: Protect data in transit and at rest
questions.title: Protect sensitive training data
questions.details: Sensitive training data should be governed, encrypted, and masked as needed before use in training.

databricksGuidance.context: Training data often contains the most sensitive data in the org.

questions: Is sensitive training data governed and protected?

questions.principle: Manage identity and access using least privilege
questions.title: Keep secrets out of training/serving code
questions.details: Credentials used in ML pipelines and endpoints must come from a secret store.

databricksGuidance.context: Secret management keeps ML credentials out of code and logs.

questions: Are secrets referenced from a scope?
Is code free of hard-coded credentials?

questions.principle: Manage identity and access using least privilege
questions.title: Control access to model endpoints
questions.details: Serving endpoints should authenticate callers and restrict who can invoke them.

databricksGuidance.context: Open model endpoints can expose predictions and, indirectly, training data.

questions.title: Audit model access and deployment changes
questions.details: Access to models and changes to deployments should be auditable.

databricksGuidance.context: Auditing model lifecycle changes supports compliance and RCA.

pillars.name: Reliability
pillars.description: Make ML dependable: reproducible training, robust serving, and recovery.

questions.title: Use scalable, production-grade model serving
questions.details: Models should be served on production-grade infrastructure that handles scale and failures.

databricksGuidance.context: Robust serving keeps ML predictions available under load.

questions.title: Configure retries and timeouts for training jobs
questions.details: Training jobs should retry transient failures and time out if they hang.

databricksGuidance.context: Retries and timeouts keep training resilient and cost-bounded.

questions.principle: Take a data-centric approach to machine learning
questions.title: Ensure reproducible training runs
questions.details: Training should be reproducible (pinned data version, params, environment) so a model can be rebuilt.

databricksGuidance.context: Reproducibility is the foundation of ML recovery and trust.

questions: Are data version and environment pinned?

questions.title: Enable rollback to a previous model version
questions.details: If a deployed model regresses, you should be able to roll back to a known-good version quickly.

databricksGuidance.context: Model rollback is the recovery path for a bad deployment.

questions: Can you roll back to a prior model version?

questions.title: Autoscale training and serving to demand
questions.details: Training and serving compute should scale with workload, including scale-to-zero for idle endpoints.

databricksGuidance.context: Autoscaling matches ML capacity to demand.

questions: Is scale-to-zero used for idle endpoints?

pillars.name: Performance Efficiency
pillars.description: Make ML efficient: right-sized compute, GPUs where needed, tuned training.

questions.title: Match hardware to the ML workload
questions.details: Choose CPU/GPU and instance types to fit the training/inference workload rather than a default.

databricksGuidance.context: Hardware fit is a major driver of ML training speed and cost.

questions: Is hardware matched to the workload?
Are GPUs used only where they help?

questions.title: Use distributed training where beneficial
questions.details: Large training jobs should use distributed/parallel training when it speeds them up.

databricksGuidance.context: Distributed training cuts wall-clock time for large jobs.

questions: Is distributed training used where beneficial?

questions.title: Use the feature store to avoid recomputing features
questions.details: Precomputed, reusable features avoid recomputing the same transformations for every model.

databricksGuidance.context: Feature reuse removes redundant computation from ML.

questions.title: Test model performance on representative data
questions.details: Latency and throughput of serving should be tested on production-like data before release.

databricksGuidance.context: Realistic testing avoids serving performance surprises.

questions: Is serving tested on representative data?

questions.title: Monitor training and inference performance
questions.details: Track training duration and inference latency/throughput to catch regressions.

databricksGuidance.context: Performance monitoring keeps ML within SLA and budget.

pillars.name: Cost Optimization
pillars.description: Control ML cost: right-sized GPUs, spot training, and idle-endpoint scaling.

questions.title: Only use GPUs for workloads that need them
questions.details: Reserve GPU compute for training/inference that genuinely benefits; use CPUs otherwise.

databricksGuidance.context: GPU misuse is a leading source of ML overspend.

questions: Are GPUs reserved for workloads that need them?

questions.title: Use job clusters for training runs
questions.details: Training should run on ephemeral job clusters that terminate when done.

databricksGuidance.context: Job clusters avoid idle-compute cost between training runs.

questions.title: Use spot/preemptible instances for tolerant training
questions.details: Fault-tolerant training can use spot instances at large discounts.

databricksGuidance.context: Spot instances cut training cost for interruptible jobs.

questions: Is spot capacity used for tolerant training?

questions.title: Scale serving endpoints to zero when idle
questions.details: Intermittent model endpoints should scale to zero so idle serving is not billed.

databricksGuidance.context: Scale-to-zero avoids paying for idle model endpoints.

questions: Do idle endpoints scale to zero?

questions.title: Attribute ML training and serving cost
questions.details: Tag ML compute so training and serving cost is attributable to models/teams.

databricksGuidance.context: Attribution makes ML spend visible and optimizable.

questions: Is ML compute tagged for attribution?
